title: Basic Calculator
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly resolving innermost parentheses by rebuilding the string versus a single-pass stack that saves the result and sign at each open group.

blocks.text: Given a string s representing a math expression made only of non negative integers, plus signs, minus signs, parentheses, and spaces, evaluate it and return the resulting integer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Working Out a Bill With Grouped Add-Ons
blocks.text: Picture reading a receipt where some charges are grouped together in brackets to show they should be combined before being added or subtracted from the rest. To get the final total, the bracketed groups need to be worked out first, and then folded into the running total using whatever sign, plus or minus, applies to that entire group.

blocks.caption: Evaluate grouped parts first, then combine everything into one total

blocks.text: The innermost group, 4 plus 5 plus 2, is 11. That makes the outer expression 1 plus 11 minus 3, which is 9.
Spaces are simply ignored, leaving 2 minus 1 plus 2, which is 3.

Nested parentheses mean this expression has a self similar structure, an inner group behaves like its own smaller expression, so it is worth asking exactly what information the outer expression actually needs to remember while an inner group is being worked out.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Resolving the innermost group first, then treating its computed value as a single number in place of the parentheses, is the natural way to think about nested expressions, and repeatedly rewriting the string does exactly this, just inefficiently.

Observation 2: What the outer expression genuinely needs to remember while an inner group is being resolved is only two numbers, the running total built up so far outside this group, and the sign this entire group needs to be combined with once it closes, nothing else about the outer context matters until the group finishes.

Observation 3: Parentheses always close in the exact reverse order they opened, the most recently opened group is always the very next one to close, which is precisely the behavior a stack provides.

Observation 4: Testing "(1+(2))" confirms it, pushing the result and sign each time a group opens, and popping them back to combine with the finished inner value each time a group closes, correctly reproduces the nested evaluation in a single left to right pass, with no rescanning of the string at all.
That reframing, a stack as a way to pause and later resume exactly two saved numbers, is what turns a repeatedly-rewritten-string simulation into a single clean pass.

Repeatedly find the innermost pair of parentheses, evaluate just the flat expression inside it, and splice that computed value directly back into the string in place of the parentheses. Once no parentheses remain, evaluate whatever flat expression is left.

items: While the string still contains an opening parenthesis, find the first closing parenthesis, and the opening parenthesis that matches it, which must be the closest one before it.
Evaluate the flat expression between that matching pair using a simple left to right pass tracking a running sign.
Replace that entire parenthesized piece, including the parentheses themselves, with its computed value.
Once no parentheses remain, evaluate the final flat expression the same way.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: repeatedly resolve the innermost parentheses, then evaluate what remains

codes.python:
def eval_flat(expr):                         # evaluate an expression with no parentheses at all
    result = 0
    num = 0
    sign = 1
    for ch in expr + "+":                        # a trailing "+" flushes the very last number
        if ch.isdigit():
            num = num * 10 + int(ch)
        elif ch in "+-":
            result += sign * num                    # apply the previous sign to the number just read
            num = 0
            sign = 1 if ch == "+" else -1
    return result


def calculate(s):
    while "(" in s:
        close = s.index(")")                      # the first closing parenthesis found
        open_ = s.rindex("(", 0, close)             # its matching opening parenthesis, just before it
        inner_value = eval_flat(s[open_ + 1:close])   # evaluate only what is inside this pair
        s = s[:open_] + str(inner_value) + s[close + 1:]  # splice the value back into the string
    return eval_flat(s)                           # no parentheses left, evaluate what remains


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "(1+(4+5+2)-3)"
    print(calculate(s))

blocks.text: This is correct, since resolving one parenthesized group at a time, from the inside out, eventually removes every group and leaves a single flat expression to evaluate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case. Each pass rescans and rebuilds a string of length up to n, and a deeply nested expression can require up to n such passes.
Space: O(n), for the string being rebuilt on every pass.

Limitation: repeatedly rescanning and rebuilding the entire string, once for every level of nesting, does a lot of duplicated work on the parts of the string that are not changing. The whole expression can instead be evaluated in a single left to right pass, remembering what to do once a parenthesis closes by saving it on a stack the moment that parenthesis opens.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeatedly rewriting the string works but is wasteful: every pass rescans the entire string again, even the parts far away from the group that just got resolved, and a deeply nested expression needs one pass per level of nesting.

What actually needs to be remembered when a group opens: just two numbers, the result accumulated so far outside the group, and the sign that entire group carries into the outer expression once it closes.

Why a stack is exactly the right structure for this: groups always close in the exact reverse order they opened, so pushing those two numbers on open and popping them on close always restores exactly the right outer context.

Can the entire expression be evaluated in a single pass this way: yes, since every parenthesis is handled the moment it is seen, with no need to ever look back at the string or rebuild it.

The core idea: track a running result and sign; on an opening parenthesis, push both and reset them to start the group fresh; on a closing parenthesis, finish the group, then pop and combine it back into the saved outer result and sign.

Walk through the string once. Track a running result and the sign currently in effect. When an opening parenthesis is seen, save the result and sign built up so far onto a stack, then start fresh for the group that is beginning. When a closing parenthesis is seen, finish the group, then combine it back into whatever was saved just before that group started.
Walk the string once, pushing the running result and sign onto a stack whenever a group opens, and popping them back to combine with the finished group whenever it closes.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: save the running result and sign on a stack whenever a group opens

codes.python:
def calculate(s):
    stack = []
    result = 0
    num = 0
    sign = 1
    for ch in s:
        if ch.isdigit():
            num = num * 10 + int(ch)
        elif ch in "+-":
            result += sign * num                    # apply the previous sign to the number just read
            num = 0
            sign = 1 if ch == "+" else -1
        elif ch == "(":
            stack.append(result)                     # remember the result built up so far
            stack.append(sign)                       # remember the sign this whole group carries
            result = 0
            sign = 1
        elif ch == ")":
            result += sign * num                     # finish the number just before this closing bracket
            num = 0
            result *= stack.pop()                     # apply the sign the group carried in from outside
            result += stack.pop()                     # add back the result from before the group started
    result += sign * num                            # flush whatever number the expression ends on
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "(1+(2))"
    print(calculate(s))

blocks.text: This works because the two values saved at every opening parenthesis, the outer result and the sign that group carries, are exactly and only what is needed to correctly fold the group's final value back into the outer expression once it closes; since groups close in the exact reverse order they opened, a stack always hands back the correct outer context, and since nothing about the string outside the current group is touched while that group is being resolved, the whole expression is evaluated correctly in a single left to right pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a genuine complexity class improvement, every character is visited exactly once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case of deeply nested parentheses, this is the real floor for this problem, since a single pass over the input is unavoidable and the stack depth genuinely reflects how deeply nested the expression is.

blocks.text: Whenever an expression can be nested inside itself, a stack is the natural way to remember "what to come back to" once the current nested part finishes, avoiding the repeated rescanning that comes from resolving one group at a time and rebuilding the string. Saving both the result so far and the sign in effect, right when a group opens, is what makes combining everything back together correct once that group closes.

items: Forgetting to flush the very last number in the expression once the loop finishes, since there is no trailing operator to trigger it.
Popping the result and sign off the stack in the wrong order when a group closes.
Not handling multi digit numbers correctly, a number can be more than one character long and must be built up digit by digit.

blocks.text: Explaining why a stack is needed here, specifically that it lets the algorithm "pause" the outer expression, fully resolve an inner group, then resume exactly where it left off, is a much stronger signal than just producing working code without explaining the reasoning behind the stack.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "why do you need a stack here", think: parentheses close in the exact reverse order they open, and a stack always hands back the correct saved outer context.
If the interviewer says "what exactly do you push", think: only the two numbers that matter, the outer result so far and the sign the group carries.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid rescanning the string", think: handle every parenthesis the moment it is seen, in a single left to right pass, with no rebuilding.

Any recursive descent expression evaluator, where the stack based iterative version here is the non recursive equivalent of resolving nested groups via function calls.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated parenthesis resolution approach runs in O(n squared) time in the worst case, rescanning and rebuilding the string once per level of nesting, using O(n) space. The single pass stack based approach runs in O(n) time, a genuine complexity class improvement, using O(n) space for the stack, the real floor for this problem.

items: Pattern: stack based expression evaluation, where opening a group pushes the outer context, and closing a group pops it back and combines it with the finished inner result.

Core Idea: only two numbers need to be saved when a group opens, the outer result so far and the sign the group carries, and since groups close in the exact reverse order they open, a stack always restores exactly the right context in a single left to right pass.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version.
Space: O(n) for both versions, for the rebuilt string in the brute force and for the stack in the optimized version.
Most Important Observation: a stack is the natural tool whenever a nested structure needs to "pause" an outer context, resolve an inner one, and resume exactly where it left off.
Interview Difficulty: easy to describe the repeated-resolution idea; identifying exactly which two values need to be pushed and popped is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: push result and sign on open, pop and combine on close, flush the last number at the very end.
